newsitem.title: CANADA: Alcan, province said close to Kemano deal.
newsitem.headline: Alcan, province said close to Kemano deal.

text.p: British Columbia and Alcan Aluminium Ltd are getting closer to a deal on compensation for Alcan's cancelled Kemano hydroelectric project and a settlement may be reached within 48 hours, British Columbia Premier Glen Clark said Tuesday.
Alcan spent C$536 million on the half-built Kemano project in northern British Columbia before the government cancelled it in 1995.

The two sides have been negotiating on compensation sporadically since then and intensively in recent weeks. The company said earlier Tuesday that they were closer to a settlement than ever before in the negotiations.
The company and province have been discussing a deal under which Alcan would receive extra power from the government-owned electric utility to expand its Kitimat smelter and increase employment.
"We're very, very close to an agreement, so we're hopeful we'll get an agreement," Clark told reporters.

Asked if a deal might be possible in 48 hours, he said: "Well, if you mean a final legal document, probably not. But if you mean...an agreement that still needs a bit of due diligence then yes, it's possible."

He reiterated previous government assertions that the deal would entail no cash for Alcan. Instead the province would supply power to the company at rates comparable to the cost of producing it at the now abandoned Kemano plant.
Clark was speaking to reporters after the Vancouver Sun newspaper quoted him as saying the province was considering legislation that would impose a settlement on the company.

Appearing to back away from that threat, Clark said legislation was an option but he was hopeful for a deal. In any event, legislation may be necessary to implement a settlement agreement but that was not yet clear, he said.

The provincial legislature is expected to recess for the summer in two days. Clark said that if legislation was "an option" then it would have to be completed by the end of the session. "We've always looked to legislation as an option. It's a matter of public record," he said.
